title: "Teaching"
comments: false
---

My teaching centers on addressing alienation, understood as the separation of students from their own ways of knowing and, subsequently, from meaningful participation in the work they are learning to do. Much of higher education remains organized around what learning scientists describe as assembly-line instruction. Four objectives guide my teaching: (1) center the knowledge of communities and the people public health serves across course content; (2) replace assembly-line instruction with learning organized around collaborative and meaningful work; (3) cultivate accessible, experiential learning where students observe and then take part in real public health work; and (4) foster critical consciousness about the social conditions that shape health and about how public health practice can change them.

In practice, I draw on the Learning by Observing and Pitching In (LOPI) Framework, a way of learning common in many Indigenous communities of the Americas that develops through participation in meaningful and shared work. Students learn methods by observing, practicing, and contributing alongside their peers and me as their instructor. These commitments serve all learners. Through these practices, I aim to reconnect students with their own ways of knowing and with meaningful participation in public health work. As students draw on community knowledge and contribute to meaningful work, they develop a sense of agency in changing the conditions that shape health.

To learn more about my teaching approach, please review my essay titled “Towards a Red Pedagogy for Social Work Education” as part of the Teaching Effectiveness Award at <https://gsi.berkeley.edu/sierra-2023/>. [[PDF]](Towards_a_Red_Pedagogy_for_Social_Work_Education.pdf)
